body: ****** ABDUL FAYAZ, J.- Through the instant criminal appeal under Section 8(A) of the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, read with Section 410 Cr.P.C., the appellants, namely Babar Qadeer, Badar Qadeer, Sohail Qadeer, Asad Qadeer, Ali Qadeer, Khalid Qadeer and Rashid Qadeer, have challenged the judgment dated 12.11.2024 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-IV, Mansehra, whereby they were convicted under Section 3 of the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, and sentenced to undergo five years' simple imprisonment each, with a fine of Rs.50,000/- each and, in default of payment thereof, to further undergo six months' simple imprisonment. They were also directed to pay compensation of Rs.100,000/- each to the complainants in equal shares under Section 544-A Cr.P.C. The connected criminal revision bearing No. 41-A/2024 has been preferred by the complainant party seeking enhancement of the sentences awarded to the appellants. Since both matters arise out of the same judgment, they are being decided through this single judgment.

2. Briefly stated, the facts giving rise to the instant appeal are that respondents No.1 and 2, namely Mst. Samar Parveen and Mst. Adeeba Bibi, instituted a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, alleging that they were in lawful possession of certain shops and a drawing room situated at Lower Dandi Shinkiari Road, Mansehra, which had been constructed by their predecessor. It was alleged that on 07.07.2022, the appellants, along with other persons, forcibly entered the disputed premises, removed the belongings of the complainants and dispossessed them without lawful authority. Upon institution of the complaint, an inquiry was conducted through the concerned police and revenue officials, who submitted their respective reports. Thereafter, the appellants were summoned to face trial and a formal charge was framed against them, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. The complainants produced evidence in support of their allegations, whereas the appellants, in their statements recorded under Section 342 Cr.P.C., denied the allegations and professed innocence. On conclusion of the trial, the learned trial Court convicted and sentenced the appellants through the impugned judgment. Feeling aggrieved, the appellants have preferred the instant appeal, whereas the complainant party has filed the connected criminal revision seeking enhancement of their sentences.

4. A careful examination of the available record reveals that the complainants were dispossessed from the disputed premises without recourse to lawful process. However, the mere establishment of unlawful dispossession is not sufficient, by itself, to sustain the conviction of the present appellants unless their involvement in the commission of the alleged offence is established through reliable and confidence-inspiring evidence. The principal question requiring determination is, therefore, whether the evidence produced by the complainants sufficiently connects the appellants with the alleged occurrence and establishes their criminal liability beyond reasonable doubt. In this regard, the prosecution evidence requires careful scrutiny, particularly when seven persons have been charged collectively in connection with the same occurrence.

5. Perusal of the complaint and the evidence brought on record reveals that the appellants have been implicated in the alleged occurrence in a general and collective manner, without clearly specifying the individual role played by each of them. The complainants have not satisfactorily explained which of the appellants actually entered the disputed premises, who removed their belongings, who forcibly expelled them or who otherwise actively participated in the alleged dispossession. The allegations are substantially omnibus in nature, and no convincing evidence has been produced to distinguish the acts of one appellant from those of the others. Although the law does not invariably require a separate overt act to be attributed to every accused where participation in furtherance of a common intention is otherwise established, the prosecution must nevertheless prove the involvement of each accused through reliable evidence. In the present case, neither their individual participation nor any legally attributable common intention has been established with the degree of certainty required for recording a criminal conviction. The mere nomination of all the appellants in the complaint, without satisfactory proof of their actual involvement, cannot be treated as sufficient evidence of guilt.

6. It is also pertinent to mention that the parties are admittedly related to each other and have been involved in litigation concerning the disputed property. The record reflects that proceedings regarding their respective claims over the property were already pending before the competent civil Court. Although the existence of a civil dispute does not authorize any party to take the law into its own hands or forcibly dispossess another person, the background of such litigation assumes significance while examining the criminal liability of the persons charged. In cases arising out of property disputes between related parties, the possibility of general implication of several family members cannot altogether be overlooked, particularly where the complainants fail to specify the precise role of each accused. The criminal Court is, therefore, required to distinguish between the factum of unlawful dispossession and the question as to who was actually responsible for committing the offence. The former may be established from the surrounding circumstances and documentary record, but the latter must be proved through evidence connecting the accused with the alleged criminal act.

7. The statements of the prosecution witnesses and the inquiry reports available on record have also been examined. The evidence may support the allegation that the complainants were unlawfully deprived of possession of the disputed premises, but it does not satisfactorily establish which of the appellants was responsible for such dispossession. The reports of the police and revenue officials primarily relate to the possession, location and status of the disputed property and do not independently establish the individual participation of the appellants in the alleged occurrence. Likewise, the statements of the witnesses do not furnish a clear and consistent account of the specific acts committed by the respective appellants. The distinction between establishing unlawful dispossession and identifying the persons criminally responsible for it appears to have escaped the attention of the learned trial Court, which placed considerable reliance upon the factum of dispossession while recording conviction against all the appellants collectively. Such an approach is not sufficient to sustain a conviction when the evidence regarding the identity and participation of the actual perpetrators remains uncertain.

8. Another important aspect of the matter is that possession of the disputed property has since been restored to the complainants. Thus, the grievance relating to deprivation of possession has been redressed to that extent. It is, however, clarified that restoration of possession does not, by itself, absolve a person of criminal liability for an offence already committed. Nevertheless, the conviction of an accused must independently rest upon proof of his involvement in the commission of the offence. In the present case, even if the factum of illegal dispossession is accepted, the available evidence does not establish beyond reasonable doubt which of the seven appellants actually participated in the alleged occurrence. In such circumstances, the fact that the complainants were unlawfully dispossessed cannot justify the conviction of all the appellants merely because they were collectively named in the complaint. Criminal liability is personal and cannot be presumed on the basis of relationship, association or collective nomination alone.

9. It is a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that the prosecution is under a legal obligation to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, and the burden cannot be shifted upon the accused to establish their innocence. It is equally settled that even a single circumstance creating reasonable doubt in the prosecution case is sufficient to entitle an accused to its benefit, which is to be extended as a matter of right and not of grace. In the present case, the absence of specific attribution, the failure to establish the individual participation of the appellants and the background of existing litigation between the parties are circumstances which, when considered together, create reasonable doubt regarding the criminal liability of the appellants. The learned trial Court, while appreciating the prosecution evidence, failed to give due consideration to these material aspects and proceeded to convict all the appellants without sufficiently determining their respective involvement in the alleged offence. The impugned judgment, therefore, suffers from misappreciation of evidence and cannot be sustained in law.

10. For the foregoing reasons, the instant criminal appeal is allowed. Consequently, the impugned judgment dated 12.11.2024 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-IV, Mansehra, to the extent of conviction and sentence of the appellants, is hereby set aside, and all seven appellants, namely Babar Qadeer, Badar Qadeer, Sohail Qadeer, Asad Qadeer, Ali Qadeer, Khalid Qadeer and Rashid Qadeer, are acquitted of the charge by extending them the benefit of doubt.

11. In view of the findings recorded hereinabove, whereby the conviction and sentences awarded to the appellants have been set aside and they have been acquitted of the charge, the connected criminal revision No. 41- A/2024 filed by the complainant party seeking enhancement of their sentences has lost its very foundation. Consequently, the said criminal revision is dismissed as having become infructuous.

12. Before parting with this judgment, it is clarified that the acquittal of the appellants shall not affect the possession already restored to the complainants, nor shall any observation made herein prejudice the rights of the parties in any pending civil proceedings concerning the disputed property, which shall be determined independently by the competent Court strictly in accordance with law.
